title_en: Annual Report of the Supreme People's Court on Intellectual Property Cases (2009) (Continued)
keywords_en: trademark rights; retrial petition; intellectual property; intellectual property case of the Supreme People's Court
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases (Continuation) (2009)

(Continued from Previous Issue)

15. Whether the use of a trademark during the period when it was included in the national drug standard may be considered in determining whether the trademark is well-known

According to Article 14 of the Trademark Law, the duration, extent, and geographical scope of any advertising of the trademark shall be considered as one of the factors in determining whether the trademark is well-known. In judicial practice, there are different views on whether the use of a registered trademark during the period when it is included in the national drug standard affects the assessment of the trademark's recognition.

In the case of petitioner Jiangxi Juyuan Pharmaceutical Bioengineering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Juyuan Company) v. respondent Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce and third party Hangzhou Minsheng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Minsheng Company) (administrative dispute over a trademark) [(2009) Zhi Xing Zi No. 12], the Supreme People's Court held that under specific historical circumstances, certain drug names were once included in national drug standards. After the drug standards were revised and such names were no longer statutory generic names for drugs, if such names have not in fact become generic names, they should still be regarded as capable of indicating the source of goods. Accordingly, when considering the recognition of such a registered trademark, factors such as the use and advertising of the registered trademark by the trademark owner during the period when it was included in the national drug standard may be taken into account.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Hangzhou Minsheng Pharmaceutical Factory, the predecessor of Minsheng Company, filed an application with the Trademark Office on January 20, 1987 for the word mark "21 Jinweita," Registration No. 297849, which was approved for registration on August 30, 1987, for use on Class 5 western medicines. Minsheng Company's "21 Jinweita" product was recognized as a famous trademark of Hangzhou City in 1989 and of Zhejiang Province in 1997, and was rated as a famous brand product of Hangzhou City and Zhejiang Province in 1998. Between 1997 and 2000, Minsheng Company conducted extensive advertising for its "21 Jinweita" trademark, including television, radio, and outdoor advertisements, covering a nationwide scope. Nanchang Huiri Health Preparation Co., Ltd., the predecessor of Juyuan Company, filed an application with the Trademark Office on December 21, 2000 for the combined trademark "21 Jinweita and Device," Registration No. 1687032, which was approved for registration on December 21, 2001, for use on Class 30 non-medical nutritional liquids and other goods. On August 8, 2002, Minsheng Company requested the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to cancel the registered trademark No. 1687032. On June 30, 2004, the Board issued a ruling [2004] No. 3021, finding that Minsheng Company's cited trademark No. 279849 had become a well-known trademark, entitled to cross-class protection, and canceled Juyuan Company's trademark No. 1687032. Juyuan Company, dissatisfied with the ruling, initiated an action. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, on December 23, 2004, rendered an administrative judgment [2004] Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 727, setting aside the Board's ruling [2004] No. 3021. Minsheng Company appealed. The Beijing High People's Court, on December 1, 2005, rendered an administrative judgment [2005] Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 122, setting aside the first-instance administrative judgment No. 727 and the Board's ruling [2004] No. 3021, and ordering the Board to render a new ruling. On May 10, 2006, the Board issued a ruling [2004] Chong No. 32, canceling Juyuan Company's registered trademark No. 1687032. Juyuan Company, dissatisfied, again initiated an action. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, after trial, sustained the Board's ruling [2004] Chong No. 32. Juyuan Company appealed. The Beijing High People's Court, after trial, sustained the first-instance judgment and dismissed Juyuan Company's appeal. Juyuan Company, dissatisfied with that judgment, petitioned the Supreme People's Court for retrial on grounds including that from 1984 to July 1, 2000, "21 Jinweita" was a generic name for goods and could not be used as a trademark, and that the original trial judgment erred in finding Minsheng Company's cited trademark to be well-known. The Supreme People's Court, on October 27, 2009, issued a ruling dismissing Juyuan Company's petition.

The Supreme People's Court found upon review that, during the period from 1984 to July 1, 2000, "21 Jinweita" became a statutory generic name due to its inclusion in the national drug standard. However, before the cited trademark was canceled through statutory procedures, Minsheng Company enjoyed the exclusive right to use the registered trademark under the law and was entitled to use the cited trademark on the approved goods. Considering factors such as the duration, geographical scope, and records of protection of Minsheng Company's advertising and use of the cited trademark, the cited trademark had reached the level of a well-known trademark at the time of the application for registration of the disputed trademark in this case. After the implementation of the National Drug Standard No. 2000 Yao Biao Zi XG-005 for Multivitamin Tablets (21) on July 1, 2000, the historical issue of whether "21 Jinweita" was a generic name for goods or a registered trademark was resolved, and the existing evidence could not prove that "21 Jinweita" had become a generic name for multivitamin tablets.

16. Consideration of the use of a trademark before its registration in determining whether the trademark is well-known

Article 14 of the Trademark Law provides that, in determining whether a trademark is well-known, the advertising and use of the trademark shall be considered. According to Article 5, paragraph 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Involving the Protection of Well-Known Trademarks, the duration, scope, and manner of use of a trademark include its continuous use before the trademark was approved and registered.

In the case of petitioner Beijing China Railway Express Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing CRE Company) v. respondent Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce and third party China Railway Express Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as CRE Company) (administrative dispute over a trademark) [(2009) Zhi Xing Zi No. 1], the Supreme People's Court held that, in determining whether a trademark is well-known, not only the use of the trademark after its registration, but also the continuous use of the trademark before its registration should be considered.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Beijing CRE Company filed an application for registration of the disputed trademark "Zhong Tie" on August 28, 1997, which was approved for registration on September 21, 1998, for services in Class 39. Beijing CRE Foreign Service Express Company filed an application for registration of the cited trademark "CRE Zhong Tie Kuai Yun" ("Kuai Yun" being outside the exclusive scope) on February 20, 1995, which was approved for registration on January 14, 1997, for services in Class 39, including delivery services (information or goods) and parcel delivery. In 1997, after China Railway Foreign Service Corporation and Beijing CRE Foreign Service Express Company jointly established China Railway Express Co., Ltd., the cited trademark was approved for assignment to China Railway Express Co., Ltd. (later renamed CRE Company). On September 12, 2003, CRE Company applied for cancellation of the registration of the disputed trademark on the ground that its registration violated Article 13, paragraph 2, Article 28, and Article 31 of the Trademark Law. On June 23, 2005, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board issued a ruling Shang Ping Zi [2005] No. 1804, finding that the cited trademark was a well-known trademark and that the registration of the disputed trademark violated Article 13, paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law and should be canceled, and ordered the cancellation of the registration of the disputed trademark. Beijing CRE Company, dissatisfied with the ruling, filed an action with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. On December 23, 2005, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered an administrative judgment (2005) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 842, setting aside the ruling [2005] No. 1804. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and CRE Company appealed. On July 21, 2006, the Beijing High People's Court rendered an administrative judgment (2006) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 261, dismissing the appeal and sustaining the original trial judgment. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board formed a new collegial panel and, on June 6, 2007, issued a ruling Shang Ping Zi [2005] Chong Shen No. 60. That ruling found that the valid evidence submitted by CRE Company within the prescribed time limit was insufficient to prove that CRE Company's cited trademark was a well-known trademark at the time of the application for registration of the disputed trademark, and therefore sustained Beijing CRE Company's disputed trademark. CRE Company, dissatisfied with that ruling, filed an action. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, at first instance, sustained the Board's ruling [2005] No. 1804 Chong Shen No. 60. CRE Company appealed. At second instance, the Beijing High People's Court found that the cited trademark had become a well-known trademark widely known by the relevant public in China before the application for registration of the disputed trademark, and therefore set aside the first-instance judgment and the Board's ruling Shang Ping Zi [2005] No. 1804 Chong Shen No. 60, and ordered the Board to render a new ruling. Beijing CRE Company, dissatisfied with that judgment, petitioned the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On September 21, 2009, the Supreme People's Court issued a ruling dismissing its petition.

The Supreme People's Court found upon review that, in determining whether a trademark is well-known, not only the use of the trademark after its registration, but also the continuous use of the trademark before its registration should be considered. According to the facts found, CRE Company was a direct subsidiary of the Ministry of Railways. Its predecessor, China Railway Express Co., Ltd., and the parent company of China Railway Express Co., Ltd., China Railway Foreign Service Corporation, were exclusively engaged in railway parcel express services in China in accordance with relevant regulations of the Ministry of Railways. Such services began on a trial basis in seven cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Shenyang, and Zhengzhou) in 1993, and were formally launched nationwide in 1997. During this period, China Railway Express Co., Ltd., its parent company China Railway Foreign Service Corporation, and their branches made extensive use and advertising of the cited trademark. Before Beijing CRE Company filed an application for registration of the disputed trademark, the cited trademark had already become widely known by the relevant public and should be recognized as a well-known trademark.

(II) Trial of Civil Trademark Cases

17. Consideration of the fact that a registered trademark has not been actually used in determining trademark similarity

According to Article 9, paragraph 2, and Article 10 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks, trademark similarity means that compared with the plaintiff's registered trademark, the allegedly infringing trademark is similar in terms of the shape, pronunciation, or meaning of the characters, or the composition or color of the device, or the overall structure of the combination of their elements, or the three-dimensional shape or color combination, so as to easily cause the relevant public to mistake the source of the goods or to believe that the source of the goods is specifically connected with the goods of the plaintiff's registered trademark. In determining trademark similarity, the general attention of the relevant public shall be the standard, and it is necessary to compare the trademarks as a whole and also compare the main parts of the trademarks, and the comparison shall be conducted in an isolated state of the compared objects. The distinctiveness and reputation of the registered trademark for which protection is sought shall also be considered.

In the case of petitioner Yunnan Chengtou Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yunnan Chengtou Company) v. respondents Shandong Taihe Century Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Taihe Investment Company) and Ji'nan Honghe Beverage Preparation Business Department (hereinafter referred to as Ji'nan Honghe Business Department) (dispute over infringement of the exclusive right to use a trademark) [(2008) Min Ti Zi No. 52, hereinafter referred to as the "Honghe" trademark infringement case], the Supreme People's Court further refined the factors to be considered in determining trademark similarity. It mainly reflected that, in determining trademark similarity for the purpose of infringement, in addition to comparing the similarity of constituent elements of the relevant trademarks such as shape, pronunciation, and meaning, attention should also be paid to whether such similarity is sufficient to cause market confusion. Therefore, factors such as the actual use of the relevant trademarks, distinctiveness, and whether there is any improper intent should be comprehensively considered.

The basic facts of the "Honghe" trademark infringement case are as follows: A third party, Daxing'anling Beiqishen Health Products Co., Ltd., obtained registration of the word mark "Honghe" on June 7, 1997, for use on beer and beverage preparations. On November 28, 2000, the Trademark Office approved the assignment of the mark to Ji'nan Honghe Business Department. Ji'nan Honghe Business Department was established on November 14, 2000, with registered capital of RMB 20,000, and its registered scope of business included wholesale and retail of beer and beverages, sales of hops, and development and sales of beer and beverage additives. Taihe Investment Company was established on April 20, 2001, with registered capital of RMB 5 million, and its scope of business included investment in high-tech and environmental protection, and sales of normal-temperature preserved alcoholic beverages and beverages. Ji'nan Honghe Business Department granted Taihe Investment Company the exclusive nationwide license to use the "Honghe" mark, which was recorded with the Trademark Office in August 2002. The predecessor of Yunnan Chengtou Company was the Yunnan Honghe Beverage Plant, established in 1982, which changed its name to Kaiyuan Guangming Brewery in May 1992, and after restructuring with approval from administrative authorities, established Yunnan Guangming Co., Ltd., which changed its name to Yunnan Honghe Guangming Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yunnan Honghe Company) on October 23, 1998. In 1999, the company publicly issued shares through the Shanghai Stock Exchange and became listed, and its enterprise type changed to a listed company. Before 2001, Yunnan Honghe Company used "Honghe" as the trade name and unregistered trademark for its beer; after 2002, it used "Honghehong" as the trade name and unregistered trademark for its beer. On July 24, 2001, the company applied to the Trademark Office for registration of the mark "Honghehong." After the Trademark Office made a preliminary approval announcement for that mark, Taihe Investment Company filed an opposition with the Trademark Office within the opposition period. In October 2007, Yunnan Honghe Company underwent major asset restructuring and changed its name to Yunnan Chengtou Company. In March 2004, Taihe Investment Company notarized the purchase of "Honghehong" beer produced by Yunnan Honghe Company from a convenience store in Chancheng District, Foshan City, Guangdong Province, and then jointly with Ji'nan Honghe Business Department filed a lawsuit with the Foshan Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province, requesting an order for Yunnan Honghe Company to cease infringing on its exclusive right to use the "Honghe" trademark and to pay compensation for economic losses of RMB 10 million. The court of first instance held that the word "Honghehong" prominently used by Yunnan Honghe Company on its products and in advertisements was similar to the "Honghe" trademark of Ji'nan Honghe Business Department, sufficient to mislead the public and cause the relevant public to mistake the source of the goods, thus infringing the plaintiffs' trademark right. A promotional banner hanging in the sales department of Yunnan Honghe Company, printed with a picture of a beer bottle and the red words "Honghe Beer," also constituted an act of trademark infringement. Based on the existing evidence, the infringement period of Yunnan Honghe Company could be determined as at least two years. Calculated according to the annual reports published by Yunnan Honghe Company, the gross profit from the "Honghehong" beer product during the infringement period was over RMB 22 million, and the amount of compensation claimed by the plaintiffs was within a reasonable range. The court of first instance thus ordered Yunnan Honghe Company to cease the infringement and pay RMB 10 million in compensation to the two plaintiffs. After Yunnan Honghe Company appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court, the court of second instance sustained the first-instance judgment. Yunnan Chengtou Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On October 21, 2008, the Supreme People's Court decided to grant a retrial of this case. During the retrial review and retrial proceedings of this case, the Supreme People's Court requested that the two respondents submit evidence of their actual use of the "Honghe" mark for producing and selling products and evidence reflecting their goodwill, but the two respondents never submitted such evidence. The Supreme People's Court held that "Honghehong" and "Honghe" did not constitute similar trademarks in the sense of trademark infringement, and that Yunnan Honghe Company's use of the "Honghehong" mark did not infringe the respondents' trademark right. Therefore, on April 8, 2009, the Court rendered a judgment setting aside the original trial judgments and instead dismissed all claims of Taihe Investment Company and Ji'nan Honghe Business Department.

In its retrial judgment, the Supreme People's Court held that, in determining whether a trademark is similar for the purpose of trademark infringement, it is necessary not only to compare the similarity of constituent elements of the relevant trademarks such as shape, pronunciation, and meaning, but also to consider whether the similarity is sufficient to cause market confusion. To this end, the determination of similarity should be made comprehensively based on the specific circumstances of the case, taking into account factors such as the actual use of the relevant trademarks, distinctiveness, and whether there is any improper intent. In this case, the characters "Honghe" in the respondents' registered trademark were the name of an administrative division at the county level or above and a well-known river name, and therefore the inherent distinctiveness of the mark as a trademark was not strong. Moreover, there was no evidence that the mark had acquired strong distinctiveness through actual use. Since the respondents' trademark had not yet actually functioned to identify the source, consumers would not associate "Honghehong" beer with the respondents. After Yunnan Honghe Company's sustained use of the "Honghehong" mark on a relatively large scale, it had already acquired a certain degree of market recognition and had formed a distinctive meaning for identifying goods. It should be considered that there was an overall distinction from the "Honghe" trademark. Applying the standard of attention of ordinary consumers, the source of "Honghehong" beer could be easily distinguished, and it should be held that such similarity was insufficient to cause confusion or mistake. Considering the actual use of the "Honghehong" mark on the bottle labels and outer packaging of Yunnan Honghe Company's products, Yunnan Honghe Company did not subjectively have any improper intent to cause confusion with the respondents' registered "Honghe" trademark. Taking the above factors into comprehensive consideration, it should be determined that the two marks were not similar trademarks, and Yunnan Honghe Company's use of the "Honghehong" mark did not infringe the respondents' trademark right.

18. Consideration of the actual use of a trademark in determining trademark similarity

In the case of petitioners Luzhou Qiannian Liquor Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Qiannian Liquor Company), Sichuan Zhuge Brewing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhuge Brewing Company), and Sichuan Zhuge Liang Liquor Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhuge Liang Liquor Company) v. respondent Sichuan Jiangkou Chun Liquor (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jiangkou Chun Group) and original trial defendants Zhou Wen and Yan Dequan (dispute over infringement of the exclusive right to use a trademark) [(2007) Min San Jian Zi No. 37-1], the Supreme People's Court, in determining whether the trademarks were similar, considered factors such as the actual use of the trademarks, particularly prior use and the specific manner of use.

19. The basic facts of the case are as follows: Qiannian Jiuye Company was registered and established on November 12, 1999, and on June 2002, it acquired the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" (诸葛亮). The "Zhu Geliang" trademark is a word mark in standard bold font arranged horizontally from left to right, and the designated goods are Class 33 alcoholic beverages (excluding beer), rice wine, wine (beverages), yellow wine, grape wine, edible alcohol, appetizer wine, brandy, distilled liquor, and fruit wine (containing alcohol). On October 28, 2002, Qiannian Jiuye Company began using the trademark, and on June 15, 2003, it entered into a trademark license contract with Zhugeliang Jiuye Company, authorizing Zhugeliang Jiuye Company to use the "Zhu Geliang" trademark (according to business registration materials, Zhugeliang Jiuye Company was registered and established on September 28, 2003). On August 1, 2003, Zhuge Niang Company was registered and established, officially producing Zhuge Niang liquor. On November 20, 2003, Qiannian Jiuye Company and Zhuge Niang Company entered into a trademark license contract, authorizing Zhuge Niang Company to use the "Zhu Geliang" trademark. On April 25, 1999, Jiangkou Chun Group (formerly Sichuan Province Pingchang County Distillery) entered into a "Product Development Agreement" with a third party, deciding to jointly develop "Zhuge Niang" liquor and use the "Zhuge Niang" mark on the product. On June 5, 1999, Jiangkou Chun Group officially produced "Zhuge Niang" liquor and subsequently sold it in the Guangdong market. From 2002 to 2004, the Zhuge Niang liquor produced by Jiangkou Chun Group was mainly sold in Guangdong, Sichuan, Hunan, and other places, with good sales volumes; the liquor had certain influence and recognition in the southern regions of China. The "Zhuge Niang" used by Jiangkou Chun Group as a product name was a combination of characters, with the three characters "Zhuge Niang" primarily in ancient seal script, incorporating features of Wei script and clerical script, with a seal-shaped outline added to the border of the characters. On September 24, 2004, Qiannian Jiuye Company, Zhugeliang Jiuye Company, and Zhuge Niang Company filed a lawsuit against Jiangkou Chun Group and other defendants at the Changsha Intermediate People's Court of Hunan Province, requesting an order that the defendants immediately cease trademark infringement and compensate for losses. Jiangkou Chun Group filed a counterclaim, alleging that the use of the "Zhu Geliang" trademark infringed upon its exclusive name rights as a well-known commodity ("Zhuge Niang") and constituted unfair competition. The court of first instance held that "Zhuge Niang liquor" possessed the exclusive name rights of a well-known commodity, while "Zhu Geliang" was a historical figure and lacked originality; its distinctiveness as a trademark was weaker. As long as the general public exercised ordinary attention, they would not easily mistake the defendant's "Zhuge Niang liquor" product as being produced and sold by the plaintiff's "Zhu Geliang" registered trademark product, nor would they confuse or misidentify the source of the goods. Jiangkou Chun Group's use of "Zhuge Niang liquor" did not constitute infringement of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" owned by Qiannian Jiuye Company and the other two companies. The three companies' proper and lawful use of the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" did not constitute infringement of Jiangkou Chun Group's exclusive name rights to "Zhuge Niang liquor" and did not constitute unfair competition. Therefore, the court dismissed the claims of both parties. Qiannian Jiuye Company, Zhugeliang Jiuye Company, and Zhuge Niang Company appealed the first-instance judgment. The Hunan High People's Court rendered a second-instance judgment dismissing the appeal and upholding the first-instance judgment. Qiannian Jiuye Company, Zhuge Niang Company, and Zhugeliang Jiuye Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, filed an application for retrial with the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on January 16, 2009, to dismiss their retrial application.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that determining whether "Zhuge Niang" constitutes a trademark similar to the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" for purposes of infringement requires a comprehensive assessment of relevant factors. First, comparing the two in terms of pronunciation, form, and meaning: "Zhu Geliang" and "Zhuge Niang" indeed share similarities in pronunciation and character composition. However, in terms of shape, the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" is a word mark in standard bold font arranged horizontally from left to right; the three characters "Zhuge Niang" used as a product name are arranged vertically from top to bottom, primarily in ancient seal script with features of Wei script and clerical script, with a seal-shaped outline added to the border. The specific manner of use is significantly different from the "Zhu Geliang" trademark. In terms of the meaning of the characters, "Zhu Geliang" is both a famous historical figure and carries the specific connotation of wisdom and resourcefulness; "Zhuge Niang" is not an independent word but a combination of "Zhuge" and "Niang" (meaning "brew"), used to refer to the name of an alcoholic beverage, and its overall meaning differs from "Zhu Geliang". In this case, the inherent unique meaning of "Zhu Geliang" makes the difference in meaning significant when analyzing and comparing the similarity between the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" and the product name "Zhuge Niang". This difference in meaning makes it easier for relevant consumers to distinguish between the two. Second, the distinctiveness of the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" and the actual use of both marks need to be considered. Due to its inherent unique meaning, the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang" generally has weaker distinctiveness when used as a registered trademark for alcoholic beverages, except where it has acquired strong distinctiveness through use. Before Qiannian Jiuye Company acquired the trademark, the "Zhu Geliang" registered trademark had not been actually used and lacked awareness. Qiannian Jiuye Company and others also failed to provide evidence that the "Zhu Geliang" registered trademark had acquired strong distinctiveness after use. Under such circumstances, the exclusionary power of the "Zhu Geliang" registered trademark against similar marks is relatively weak. Although the product name "Zhuge Niang" is similar to it in pronunciation and character composition, this is insufficient to establish similarity for purposes of trademark infringement. Moreover, before the "Zhu Geliang" trademark was applied for registration, Jiangkou Chun Group had already used "Zhuge Niang" as a product name, with no intent to ride on the reputation of the "Zhu Geliang" registered trademark. Before the "Zhu Geliang" trademark was approved for registration, the "Zhuge Niang" liquor had already gained initial scale and enjoyed relatively high recognition in Guangdong, Sichuan, Hunan, and other places, being known to relevant consumers, and had acquired a certain degree of distinctiveness and independent ability to distinguish the source of the goods through use. Considering the font characteristics and specific manner of use of the product name "Zhuge Niang", and the weak distinctiveness of the registered trademark "Zhu Geliang", relevant consumers, exercising ordinary attention, would not be confused or misled.

19. The meaning of trademark use in the context of trademark infringement

Article 52 of the Trademark Law provides that using a trademark identical or similar to a registered trademark on the same or similar goods without the permission of the trademark registrant constitutes infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. However, for purposes of trademark infringement, the use of a trademark must serve to identify the source and the producer as a necessary condition.

In the case of the retrial applicants Pfizer Products Inc. and Pfizer Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. v. the respondent Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Lianhuan Company") and the original defendant Guangzhou Weier Man Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Weier Man Company") concerning a dispute over trademark infringement [(2009) Minshen Zi No. 268], the Supreme People's Court held that use that cannot serve to identify the source and the producer cannot be deemed as use in the trademark sense, and such use by another party does not constitute use of an identical or similar trademark and does not constitute infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: On May 28, 2003, a three-dimensional diamond-shaped trademark in blue, designated for colors and applied by Pfizer Products Inc. to the China Trademark Office, was approved for registration with designated goods in Class 5, including pharmaceutical preparations. On March 10, 2005, Pfizer Products Inc. licensed Pfizer Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. to use the three-dimensional trademark. On June 2, 1998, Weier Man Company applied to the Trademark Office for registration of the word trademark "Viagra" (伟哥), with designated goods including human-use pharmaceuticals. The trademark was preliminarily published for opposition by the Trademark Office in April 2002. In April 2004, the trademark was transferred to Guangzhou Weier Man New Drug Development Center Co., Ltd. On January 5, 2005, Guangzhou Weier Man New Drug Development Center Co., Ltd. entered into a trademark license contract with Lianhuan Company, authorizing Lianhuan Company to use the "Viagra TM" trademark on phentolamine mesylate dispersible tablets. The phentolamine mesylate dispersible tablets produced by Lianhuan Company were packaged in boxes, with the tablets individually wrapped in opaque material printed with the words "Viagra" and "TM" and "Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd." The tablets were light blue, diamond-shaped like a compass pointer, and marked with "Viagra" and "TM." On October 11, 2005, Pfizer Products Inc. and Pfizer Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. filed a lawsuit alleging that the aforementioned acts infringed their exclusive right to use the registered trademark, requesting an order that New Concept Company immediately cease sales, and that Lianhuan Company and Weier Man Company immediately cease manufacturing and selling the infringing goods and manufacturing the trademark label in question, and assume other civil liability. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held in the first instance that the acts of Lianhuan Company and New Concept Company constituted infringement of Pfizer Products Inc.'s trademark right and ordered the two companies to bear infringement liability. Lianhuan Company appealed. The Beijing High People's Court held in the second instance that although the accused infringing drug was similar to the three-dimensional trademark in issue, consumers would not be confused when purchasing the drug, nor would they mistakenly believe the drug had some connection with the two plaintiffs. The relevant acts of Lianhuan Company and others did not constitute infringement of Pfizer Products Inc.'s trademark right, nor did they harm the interests of Pfizer Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. The court thus reversed the first-instance judgment and dismissed the claims of the two plaintiffs. The two plaintiffs appealed, and the Supreme People's Court ruled on June 24, 2009, to dismiss their retrial application.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that in this case, although the packaging of the phentolamine mesylate dispersible tablets produced by Lianhuan Company had a diamond-shaped protrusion corresponding to the shape of the tablet, and the packaging box had a yellow-brown diamond pattern as a background for the word "Viagra," consumers when purchasing the drug could not thereby identify the external shape of the drug. Since the tablets were packaged in opaque material, their color and shape could not serve to identify their source or producer, and could not be deemed as use in the sense of trademark infringement. Even if the external shape of the drug was identical or similar to the three-dimensional trademark of Pfizer Products Inc., consumers when purchasing the drug would not be confused with the three-dimensional trademark of Pfizer Products Inc., nor would they mistakenly believe the drug had some connection with Pfizer Products Inc. or Pfizer Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.

20. Consideration of historical factors when judging fair use of a trademark

Fair use of a trademark is not only a limitation on the scope of exclusion of trademark rights but also key to correctly delineating the boundaries of trademark rights and safeguarding legitimate public interests. In 2009, the Supreme People's Court further developed the factors to be considered in determining fair use of a trademark in individual rulings and refined the criteria for determining such use.

In the case of the retrial applicant Goubuli Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Goubuli Group") v. the respondent Tianfengyuan Restaurant of Jinan Grand View Garden Mall (hereinafter "Tianfengyuan Restaurant") concerning a dispute over trademark infringement [(2008) Minsan Jian Zi No. 10-1], the Supreme People's Court held that when determining whether the use of another party's registered trademark constitutes fair use, relevant historical factors should be fully considered and respected; at the same time, necessary and appropriate restrictions on the use should be imposed based on the principle of fairness.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: the predecessor of Goubuli Group registered the word trademark "Goubuli" on October 7, 1994, with designated services in Class 42, namely restaurants, banquet preparation, fast-food restaurants, and self-service restaurants. On December 29, 1999, the trademark was recognized as a well-known trademark. Tianfengyuan Restaurant opened for business in 1973, primarily dealing in steamed buns stuffed with pork and soup, and in September and November 1986, added business items such as "Goubuli" pork-stuffed soup buns. Since the 1980s, Tianfengyuan Restaurant has continuously operated "Goubuli" flavored pork soup buns. In April 2005, the "Goubuli Pork Soup Buns" operated by Tianfengyuan Restaurant were rated as "Jinan Famous (Flavor) Snack" by the Jinan Trade Service Bureau and the Jinan Catering Industry Association. In the same year, "Goubuli Pork Soup Buns" were included in the "Jinan Consumption Guide" of the Jinan Consumers' Association. The book "Jinan Time-honored Brands" published in August 1990 records that "Goubuli" buns in Jinan began to be sold from the early 1940s and remained popular until the liberation of Jinan in 1948. Especially after the liberation of Jinan, Tianfengyuan Restaurant was always busy with customers. Tianfengyuan Restaurant always hung a signboard featuring "Goubuli" pork soup buns at its entrance, with "Goubuli" pork soup buns as its main brand, and also hung a black signboard with the three characters "Goubuli" at the stairway entrance. On October 16, 2006, Goubuli Group filed a lawsuit, alleging that Tianfengyuan Restaurant's acts infringed its registered trademark right for "Goubuli" and requested an order that Tianfengyuan Restaurant cease infringement, eliminate effects, and compensate for losses. The Jinan Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province held in the first instance that Tianfengyuan Restaurant had a long history of operating "Goubuli pork soup buns" in the specific region of Jinan, did not exceed the original region or service items, and did not use the specific writing style of Goubuli Group's "Goubuli" trademark. Its use of "Goubuli" to introduce and promote the "Goubuli buns" operated under the name of Tianfengyuan Restaurant did not constitute infringement of the exclusive right to use the "Goubuli" service trademark. The court dismissed Goubuli Group's claims. Goubuli Group appealed. The Shandong High People's Court held in the second instance that Tianfengyuan Restaurant had a long history of using the word "Goubuli" as the name of one of its dishes and operating "Goubuli pork soup buns" in the specific region of Jinan. The provision of "Goubuli pork soup buns" by Tianfengyuan Restaurant was not an intentional use of the three characters "Goubuli" after Goubuli Group's trademark was registered and became well-known to compete for the market; it did not violate generally accepted business ethics and lacked subjective intent to free-ride on the reputation of the "Goubuli" service trademark; it constituted prior use. However, Tianfengyuan Restaurant's use of the three characters "Goubuli" on promotional signboards, wall advertisements, and directional signs, with prominent use of the three characters or the separation of the three characters from the name "Tianfengyuan Restaurant," could easily confuse consumers. To regulate market order and fully protect the well-known trademark "Goubuli," Tianfengyuan Restaurant must cease using the three characters "Goubuli" on promotional signboards, wall advertisements, etc., but could retain the dish name "Goubuli pork soup buns." The court thus reversed the first-instance judgment, ordering Tianfengyuan Restaurant to cease using the three characters "Goubuli" for promotion on signboards, wall advertisements, and other advertising forms; and dismissed Goubuli Group's other claims. Goubuli Group, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, filed an application for retrial with the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on February 5, 2009, to dismiss the retrial application.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that considering the historical fact that Tianfengyuan Restaurant had continuously used the dish name "Goubuli pork soup buns" before Goubuli Group registered the "Goubuli" service trademark, Tianfengyuan Restaurant could retain the dish name "Goubuli pork soup buns," but based on the principle of fairness, Tianfengyuan Restaurant must not engage in any other expansive use.

21. Judgment on fair use of descriptive trademarks

Because the words of a descriptive trademark are themselves descriptive and cannot directly serve to distinguish the source of the goods, the scope of the right to prohibit others from using it is subject to greater limitations. Pursuant to Article 49 of the Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law, where a registered trademark contains the generic name, design, or model of the goods, or directly indicates the quality, main raw materials, function, purpose, weight, quantity, or other characteristics of the goods, or contains a place name, the owner of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark has no right to prohibit others from fair use.

In the case of the retrial applicant Zhangzhou Hongning Household Chemicals Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Hongning Company") v. the respondent Zhangzhou Pien Tze Huang Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Pien Tze Huang Company") concerning a dispute over trademark infringement [(2009) Minshen Zi No. 1310], the Supreme People's Court held that when a registered trademark is descriptive, if a producer, for the purpose of explaining or objectively describing the characteristics of the goods, marks it in a good-faith manner to the necessary extent, and such marking does not cause relevant consumers to regard it as a trademark and thus confuse the source, it constitutes fair use; in judging whether the use is in good faith and necessary, factors such as business conventions may be referenced.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Pien Tze Huang Company owns the registered trademarks "PIEN TZE HUANG" (片仔癀) and "PIEN TZE HUANG" in Class 3 for toothpaste and cosmetics and Class 5 for pharmaceuticals. In 1999, the trademark "PIEN TZE HUANG" used on pharmaceutical products was recognized as a well-known trademark. Hongning Company produced and sold 27 kinds of cosmetics and daily chemical products, including "Lizhi brand PIEN TZE HUANG Pearl Cream (ointment)" and "PIEN TZE HUANG Special Effect Toothpaste," all of which used "PIEN TZE HUANG" as part of the product name and prominently used "PIEN TZE HUANG" and "PIEN TZE HUANG" on the packaging and decoration, with a font basically identical to Pien Tze Huang Company's registered trademark. On April 20, 2007, Pien Tze Huang Company filed a lawsuit, requesting an order that Hongning Company immediately cease infringement, publicly apologize, and compensate for losses. The Zhangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Fujian Province held in the first instance that Hongning Company's acts infringed Pien Tze Huang Company's exclusive right to use the registered trademark. After appeal, the Fujian High People's Court upheld the first-instance judgment. Hongning Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied for retrial with the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on October 27, 2009, to dismiss the retrial application.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that PIEN TZE HUANG is the name of a pharmaceutical product. If the accused product contains PIEN TZE HUANG ingredients, and the producer marks it in a good-faith manner to the necessary extent for the purpose of explaining or objectively describing the characteristics of the product, and such marking does not cause relevant consumers to regard it as a trademark and thus confuse the source, it may be deemed fair use. In judging whether the use is in good faith and necessary, factors such as business conventions may be referenced. If Hongning Company intended to explain that its products contained PIEN TZE HUANG ingredients, it should have marked them in an appropriate manner according to business conventions. However, in this case, Hongning Company prominently marked the words "PIEN TZE HUANG" and "PIEN TZE HUANG" in a prominent position on the packaging and decoration of the goods it produced and sold, with the marking significantly larger than Hongning Company's own trademark and other markings, and the font used was basically the same as the registered trademark of Pien Tze Huang Company. This manner of use exceeded the limits of fair use for explaining or objectively describing the goods; subjectively, it could hardly be considered in good faith, and given that Pien Tze Huang Company's registered trademark already enjoyed high recognition, it could objectively cause relevant consumers to confuse the source of the goods. Hongning Company's claim that its use constituted fair use could not be sustained.

22. Effect of the Intent and Conduct of the User of a Mark on Its Protection as an Unregistered Trademark

For an unregistered trademark mark, a certain degree of legal protection may be obtained based on the trademark's reputation arising from use. However, a person claiming rights to such a mark must have actually used the mark and have the intent to use the mark as a trademark.

In the case of Pfizer Ltd. (hereinafter Pfizer), Pfizer Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (hereinafter Pfizer Pharmaceuticals) as applicants for retrial v. Shanghai Dongfang Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Dongfang Company) Bankruptcy Liquidation Group, and the original trial defendants Beijing Health New Concept Pharmacy Co., Ltd. (hereinafter New Concept Company) and Guangzhou Weier Man Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Weier Man Company) — dispute over unfair competition and infringement of unregistered well-known trademark rights [(2009) Min Shen Zi No. 313], the Supreme People's Court held that where the applicants for retrial expressly acknowledged that they had never used a certain mark in China, the fact that others had conducted relevant publicity and other acts in relation to the mark could not be deemed to reflect the applicants' genuine intent to use the mark as a trademark. Therefore, the mark could not be found to constitute an unregistered trademark, and even less could it be found to constitute an unregistered well-known trademark.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: On November 28, 1997, Pfizer's trademark No. 1130739, the word mark "VIAGRA", was registered in China. On January 28, 2001, the mark was assigned to Pfizer Products Inc. On September 29, 1998, the *Health News* reported that "Weige (Viagra)" was the trade name of sildenafil citrate. From October 16, 1998 to September 28, 2003, 26 reports excerpted from more than 20 newspapers, including the *Haikou Evening News*, mostly referred to "Viagra" as "Weige", and referred to the producer of "Weige (VIAGRA)" as Pfizer or Pfizer Pharmaceutical Factory. The content of the reports mainly consisted of introductions and comments by the media on the efficacy, sales, and side effects of "Viagra". The *New Age Chinese-English Dictionary* (2000 edition, p. 1601; 2002 edition, p. 1232) explained the entry "Weige" as: "Weige, also called 'Wei Er Gang' Viagra, 'Wan Ai Ke' Viagra, a U.S. pharmaceutical trademark used for treating male dysfunction." On January 28, 2001, Pfizer assigned the "VIAGRA" word mark to Pfizer Products Inc. On March 17, 2005, Qiu Hongyan, an agent of the Patent and Trademark Office of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, purchased four boxes of the drug "Weige" at New Concept Company through notarization. The "Weige" product was manufactured by Dongfang Company and sold by New Concept Company. Dongfang Company was authorized by Weier Man Company to use the "Weige" trademark. On October 11, 2005, Pfizer and Pfizer Pharmaceuticals filed a lawsuit with the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court on the grounds of unfair competition and infringement of unregistered well-known trademark rights. At the first-instance trial, the two plaintiffs admitted that they had never used the "Weige" trademark in Mainland China. The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that the two plaintiffs could not prove that "Weige" was their unregistered well-known trademark and therefore did not enjoy any legal rights or interests in that mark under the Trademark Law, and accordingly rejected all their claims. The two plaintiffs appealed. The Beijing High People's Court agreed with the reasoning of the first-instance judgment and affirmed the judgment. Pfizer and Pfizer Pharmaceuticals, dissatisfied with the judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on June 24, 2009, to reject their application for retrial.

The Supreme People's Court found upon review that, since Pfizer had assigned the "VIAGRA" word mark to Pfizer Products Inc. on January 28, 2001, Pfizer was not the owner of the "VIAGRA" word mark at the time of filing the first-instance complaint and throughout the entire litigation process. Therefore, Pfizer had no rights or interests in the "VIAGRA" word mark or in the Chinese translation "Weige" that it claimed. Although multiple media outlets had associated "Weige" with "Viagra" in their reports, those reports were made by the media and were not publicity by Pfizer or Pfizer Pharmaceuticals for their own trademark. Moreover, Pfizer Pharmaceuticals had expressly declared that "Wan Ai Ke" was its official product name and admitted that it had never used the "Weige" trademark in Mainland China. Therefore, it could not be found that the media's use of "Weige" to refer to "Viagra" reflected the genuine intent of Pfizer and Pfizer Pharmaceuticals to use "Weige" as a trademark at that time. The existing evidence was insufficient to prove that "Weige" was an unregistered trademark, and even less could it prove that it was an unregistered well-known trademark.

IV. Trial of Competition Cases

23. Relationship Between an Operator's Illegal Business Conduct and Unfair Competition Conduct Giving Rise to Civil Liability

If an operator's business conduct violates the relevant provisions of administrative licensing laws and regulations, it constitutes illegal business conduct. There is some overlap between illegal business conduct and civil torts, including unfair competition conduct as defined in the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. However, not all illegal business conduct constitutes a civil tort or unfair competition conduct giving rise to civil liability.

In the appeal case of Beijing Golden Holiday Travel Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Golden Holiday Company) v. Ctrip Computer Technology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Ctrip Computer Company), Shanghai Ctrip Business Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Ctrip Business Company), Hebei Kanghui International Air Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Kanghui Service Company), and Beijing Ctrip International Travel Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Beijing Ctrip Company) — dispute over false publicity [(2007) Min San Zhong Zi No. 2, hereinafter the "Ctrip" judgment case], the Supreme People's Court clarified the relationship between illegal business conduct, civil torts, and unfair competition conduct under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. At the same time, through the ruling in this case, the Supreme People's Court affirmed the legality of the new business model of providing air ticket booking services through "Ctrip.com" by Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company, thereby protecting business model innovation and stimulating market competition.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: From July to September 2006, Golden Holiday Company filed a lawsuit and subsequently added defendants and claims, alleging that Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company had not obtained the qualification to act as civil aviation passenger ticket sales agents in accordance with the law but had actually engaged in ticket sales agency business through "Ctrip.com", which constituted illegal business conduct and also constituted false publicity; that Kanghui Service Company, although having obtained the "Approval Certificate for Civil Aviation Passenger Sales Agency Business", provided ticket issuance and delivery services for Ctrip Computer Company in the Shijiazhuang area of Hebei Province, which was an illegal transfer of administrative license and assistance in illegal business conduct and false publicity; and that the domestic ticket sales of Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company were collected by Beijing Ctrip Company, which also constituted assistance in illegal business conduct. Therefore, Golden Holiday Company requested the court to order Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company to cease the false publicity; order Ctrip Computer Company to cease all business operations conducted through "Ctrip.com (www.ctrip.com)"; and compensate the plaintiff for losses caused by the unfair competition. The Hebei High People's Court held at first instance that the alleged conduct did not constitute false publicity, and accordingly rendered judgment (2006) Ji Min San Chu Zi No. 3-2, dismissing the claims in the part of the case being adjudicated. Golden Holiday Company appealed, and on October 22, 2009, the Supreme People's Court rendered judgment dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment. As for other alleged conduct by Golden Holiday Company, which involved issues of duplicative litigation, the Hebei High People's Court separately rendered a ruling (2006) Ji Min San Chu Zi No. 3-1 dismissing the claims. Golden Holiday Company also appealed that ruling, and on the same day the Supreme People's Court issued a ruling dismissing the appeal and affirming the original ruling (see the "Ctrip" ruling case below).

The Supreme People's Court held that, in determining whether a person is actually engaged in air ticket sales agency business, the criterion should be the issuer indicated on the ticket, and operators who provide ticket-related booking, delivery, and collection services should not be treated as sales agents under the former *Regulations on the Administration of Civil Aviation Transport Sales Agencies* (i.e., Civil Aviation Order No. 37). The issues debated by the parties — whether "booking" is a part of "sales", whether "ticket booking" and "ticket delivery" also constitute "ticket sales", and whether directly collecting passenger ticket payments constitutes "selling tickets" — had no substantive significance for determining whether the conduct violated the provisions of Civil Aviation Order No. 37. Based on the existing evidence in this case, it could not be directly found that Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company had engaged in illegal civil aviation passenger ticket sales agency business. Even assuming the conduct constituted illegal business conduct in violation of administrative licensing laws and regulations, it generally would be a matter of administrative or even criminal liability, to be examined and determined by the relevant administrative authorities or criminal justice authorities. Only when an illegal business conduct violates administrative licensing laws and regulations and simultaneously constitutes a civil tort does the question of civil liability arise. In other words, illegal business conduct does not automatically equal a civil tort; a plaintiff in a civil action cannot rely solely on the fact that the defendant engaged in illegal business conduct to fulfill the burden of proof for a civil tort. Furthermore, regardless of whether an operator engages in illegal business conduct in violation of administrative licensing laws and regulations, the question of whether the operator bears civil liability for unfair competition arises only if the operator's conduct also violates the provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law and causes harm to the lawful rights and interests of other operators.

24. Whether a Company's Abbreviated Name May Be Protected Under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law

Pursuant to Article 5, Item (3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, the unauthorized use of another person's enterprise name or personal name, causing the public to mistake the goods for those of that other person, constitutes unfair competition. Article 6 of the Supreme People's Court's *Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Trials of Civil Unfair Competition Cases* provides that a trade name in an enterprise name that has a certain degree of market recognition and is known to the relevant public may be recognized as an "enterprise name" under Article 5, Item (3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. However, the above provisions do not expressly state whether a company's abbreviated name may be protected under Article 5, Item (3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

In the case of Shandong Shanqi Heavy Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Shanqi Heavy Industry Company) as applicant for retrial v. Shandong Crane Factory Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Shandong Crane Factory) — dispute over infringement of enterprise name rights [(2008) Min Shen Zi No. 758], the Supreme People's Court held that an abbreviated name of an enterprise or enterprise name that has a certain degree of market recognition, is well known to the relevant public, and has actually acquired the function of a trade name may be regarded as an enterprise name and may be protected under Article 5, Item (3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Shandong Crane Factory and Shanqi Heavy Industry Company are both enterprises primarily engaged in the crane business, located in Qingzhou City, Shandong Province. Shandong Crane Factory was established in 1968; in 1976, it was reorganized as Yidu Crane Factory; on October 31, 1991, its name was changed to Shandong Crane Factory; and on January 8, 2002, its name was again changed to Shandong Crane Factory Co., Ltd. In its corporate publicity videos, factory buildings, employee uniforms, external contracts, and other promotional and business activities, Shandong Crane Factory had long and actively used the abbreviated name "Shanqi", and its customers also commonly referred to it as "Shanqi". Shanqi Heavy Industry Company pre-approved its current enterprise name on January 13, 2004, and was formally established on February 13, 2004. On July 11, 2005, Shandong Crane Factory filed a lawsuit, requesting that Shanqi Heavy Industry Company be ordered to immediately cease using the "Shanqi" trade name and to compensate for losses. The Weifang Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province held at first instance that "Shanqi" was a specific abbreviated name of Shandong Crane Factory, that Shanqi Heavy Industry Company had infringed Shandong Crane Factory's name rights, and granted Shandong Crane Factory's claims. On appeal, the Shandong High People's Court, on the basis of finding that "Shanqi" was a specific abbreviated name of Shandong Crane Factory, held that the use of "Shanqi" in Shanqi Heavy Industry Company's enterprise name was likely to cause confusion and constituted unfair competition, thereby affirming the first-instance judgment. Shanqi Heavy Industry Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court ruled on April 27, 2009, to reject the application for retrial.

The Supreme People's Court held that abbreviated names of enterprise names arise from the convenience of linguistic communication. The formation of an enterprise's abbreviated name involves two processes: first, the enterprise itself uses the abbreviation to replace its formal name; second, the public recognizes the abbreviation, i.e., recognizes that the abbreviated name refers to the same enterprise as the formal name. Because an abbreviation omits certain qualifying elements in the formal name, it may unduly expand the scope of objects referred to by the formal name. Therefore, whether an enterprise's abbreviated name can specifically identify that enterprise depends on whether that abbreviated name is recognized by the relevant public and has established a stable association with the enterprise. An abbreviated name of an enterprise or enterprise name that has a certain degree of market recognition, is well known to the relevant public, and has actually acquired the function of a trade name may be regarded as an enterprise name. If, through use and public recognition, a specific abbreviated name of an enterprise has gained recognition among the relevant public in a specific region, has corresponding market recognition, and has established a stable connection with the enterprise, producing a commercial mark significance that identifies the business operator, then if another person later uses that enterprise's abbreviated name without authorization, and such use is sufficient to cause confusion among the relevant public in that specific region as to the identity of the market participants (the later user versus the prior enterprise), the later user will improperly exploit the prior enterprise's goodwill, infringing upon the prior enterprise's lawful rights and interests. In such circumstances, the specific abbreviated name of the prior enterprise shall be regarded as its enterprise name and shall be protected under Article 5, Item (3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law.
